title: SYSK Selects: How Does a Diving Bell Work?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun (originally aired August 8, 2012) in which Josh and Chuck explain how diving bells work. They trace the history from Aristotle's fourth-century BC description and the legend of Alexander the Great using one at the Siege of Tyre, through Denis Papin's bellows-fed fresh air, Edmund Halley's pressurized barrel system, the caissons used for the Brooklyn Bridge, and John Smeaton's mechanized air pump. They cover the physics of trapped air, nitrogen and decompression sickness (the bends), and the 2019-era story of Harrison Okene surviving 60 hours in a trapped air pocket after a tugboat sinking. The episode closes with a Sharknado tangent and listener mail from a first-year teacher.

segments.title: Opening banter and Selects introduction
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this week's Selects pick, the August 2012 episode on diving bells. The hosts exchange opening banter about the warm studio and Chuck's old article writing style.

segments.title: Ancient diving bells and Aristotle
segments.summary: The hosts describe diving bells as a precursor to scuba, with early uses and deaths. Aristotle described the principle in the fourth century BC. They discuss the legend of Alexander the Great using a bell at the Siege of Tyre and the basic physics of inverted vessels trapping air.

segments.title: Design, weight and the bends
segments.summary: The hosts explain that bells must be heavy and balanced so they do not tip, that compressed air at depth dissolves nitrogen into the blood, and that rising too fast causes decompression sickness, which can cause strokes, joint pain, and crippling.

segments.title: Fresh air and pressurized diving bells
segments.summary: Denis Papin introduced hoses and bellows to supply fresh air in the late 1600s. Edmund Halley later used weighted wooden barrels with faucets to pressurize the bell, allowing deeper and longer dives.

segments.title: Caissons and the Brooklyn Bridge
segments.summary: Caissons, large pressurized diving-bell-like structures, were used to build the Brooklyn Bridge towers. Workers suffered ear damage and decompression sickness, and project manager Washington Roebling was left crippled.

segments.title: Smeaton's air pump and early underwater work
segments.summary: John Smeaton invented a mechanical air pump operated from the surface, allowing larger bells with windows and electric lights. Such bells were used for construction, dock repair, and by saboteurs cutting anchor lines.

segments.title: Harrison Okene's 60 hours in a trapped air pocket
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Harrison Okene, a cook who survived 60 hours in a trapped air pocket after his tugboat capsized and sank about 100 feet. They explain carbon dioxide buildup as the usual killer, Boyle's law, and water absorbing CO2.

segments.title: Sharknado tangent and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about Sharknado and claim invention credit, then Chuck mentions the article and the hosts sign off with social media and contact information.
